‘THE LEGACY OF INNER ASIA

‘The current, far from adequate state of aur knowledge of the pre-history
‘of Central and Innee Asia, the presomed "Urheiovet! of the Altaie and hence
‘Turkic peoples, does not permit us to delineate their primordial territory
with any degree af precision, Although much excellent archaevlogical work
has heen done, the material finds of pre-historie, pre-literate peoples cannot
well us, without considerable corroborating, but aonetheless circumstantial,
evidence, the ethno linguistic affiliations of this or that group. All1oo often a
particular culture is aseribed to one or another ethnic grouping on the basis
of the racial types of the population connected with the finds, It has become
axiomatic, particularly in Soviet scholarship, that Mongoloid implies Turkic
or, more broadly speaking, Altaic and Buropoid non-Altaic, In dealing with
che modern populations of Central and inuet Asia, such a rigid approach is
particularly risky. The Yagnobi, for example, linguistic descendants of the
Sogdians, evince a clear Mongoloid admixture. While scholars are quite
willing 1a accept this as the result of population-mixing over the centuries,
there is a tendency to view earlier populations as somehow pristine
tepreseatatives of certain anthropological types associated with certai
languages. Languages, however, particularly in Eurasia, move about with
highly mobile populations and through political domination can exend
‘beyond ethnic and racial borders. In some instances, Tanguagc shifts could
oceur in connection with economic changes, The adoption of nomadiem, for
example, could lead to the replacement of one language by another.
Bilingualism was far from uncommon. The eatly nomads, it appears, show
considerable mixing. The configurations of these mixtures may be different
from or found in different proportions among present day populations
deriving irom these groups, but the principle that lmguage and race arc
indopendoat variables is, aeverlheless,jast as true, Tt should further be noted
in this convection that racial typing on the hasis of skeletal remains is not as,
exact a science as some of its practitioners claim. We may louk with
somewhat mote confidence to modera biological anthropology which, in
‘ime, will undoubtedly give us the answers we seek. For the present, these
data must be used with caution. In the discussion that follows, then,
refercaces to Europoid and Mongoloid, in some instances difficult categories
to determine, should uot be taken as proof positive of linguistic affiliations
Whatever may have been the racial type of the earliest Turkic-speakers
(seemingly Mongoloid), itis more than likely that they were mixed with other
elements from the opening pages of their history.

THE EARLY TURKIC PFOPLES OF WESTERN EURASIA

The Western Eurasian or Ponto-Catpian steppelands constitute one of the
principal habitation zunes of the Eurasian nomads, alongside those of
Central and Inner Asia. All three zones looked toward the rich sedentary
states and societies to their south for trade, plunder and occasionally military
employment. Of the three zunes, the steppes of Central Asia were largely
oricnted toward the Iranian oasis city-stales of the southern agrarian fringe
of the region, Iran itself and on occasion China, It was the beneficiary of
commercial contacts aud cultural influences stemming from Iran (aad more
distantly the Mediterranean world), Chiaa and the Indian subcontinent, The
Inner Asian nomads of the Mongolian steppes, as we have seen, were drawn
to the riches and culture of Ching and the Iranian and Tokharian oasis city-
states of Eastern Turkistan. The economic and cultural focus of the nomads
of Western Eurasia was largely directed toward and divided benween the
‘Roman world as represented by the Late Roman or Byzantine Erupire and
later the Christianized Slavic and Hungarian states of Eastern Furope, and
the civilizations of the non-Roman, Irano-Semitic Near Gast ic. the Sasnid
Empire aud its successor state the Arabian Caliphate. Transcauesia, whose
history was profoundly influenced by the Turkic peoples, was one of the
strategic foci of this Westem Hurasian world, botly contested by the Great
Powers om its borders.

From the nomadic perspective, Westura Eurasia was ideal territory. Its
pasturages were extensive and excellent. It fronted on important sedentary
cultures with which it could trade or eaid as circumstances dictated. It was
‘both spacious, providing the room for maneuver and retreat that nomadic
defense siratagoms required and sufficiendy distast from the centers of
military power of the sedentarist states ta remave, for the most patt, the fear
of sustained attack from that quarter. The Byzantizes never mounted an
expedition of their own into the area. The Arabs, with the exception of one
dating raid to the Middle Volga, were understandably reluctant 10 venture
beyond their Caucasian defenses, The Kus’ state centered ut Kiev (late 9th-
early 13th century) inad the capacity to infliet serious damage on the aomads.
On a mumber of occasians it did so, destroying several nomadic polities. But,
Rus’ became increasingly caught up in its own internecine strife and less
frequenily, albeit sumclimes devastatingly, focused on the steppe, Thus, on.
the whole, there was litde in theit immediate circumstances to compel the
nomads of this region, especially in the period priot to the formation of the
Rus’ state, to create forms of political organization more advaneed than the
tribal union, Statehood, in this region, was invariably imposed from without,
usnally introduced by nomadic conquerors coming from the East.

‘The Seljuk state, created by the fighting power of nomads, was aot &
nomadie state, but rather a nomadie dynasty grafted ont a traditional
Middle Eastern state. The bureauersic infrastructure was Iranian, a radition
that went back not only to alder Turkic polities, but had! equally strong roots
in the Middle East, The governmental institutions of their CAbbasid,
Enwayhid and Ghamavid precedessors were retained and sometimes
reworked. The sedentarization of the dynasty meant that eventually the
nomads would either have to beeome "good" subjects (and sedentarize) or be
perpetually at udds with the drmasty. The state, in any event, soon came to
rely on galms403 (largely. hut not exchusively nf Turkic, steppe origin) and
the role of the Oguz or Turkmen tribesmen was diminished. The institution
of the igtd®, so important for the regime's military scrvitors, was further
elaborated, perhaps in some measure to reduce the tendencies of tbe
tuihesmen towards rebellion and to provide an ecouwimic base for a new kind
of army that was not dependent on the anarchic tribes. Clearly, from the
